subtopic: Using AI tools inside a team
subtype: Approach: checking against a source of truth [Thinking]
passage: Supervisor's note. I sat in on Vaibhav's prep for the client summary on Wednesday. The AI summary of the industry report read smoothly and carried three figures and two citations. Vaibhav said aloud, 'These tools sometimes invent things that sound right, so I'll check each one against the original.' Vaibhav opened the report and went through them one by one. Two figures matched. One number was off, 14 where the report said 41, and a citation pointed to a paper Vaibhav could not find at all. Both were removed. Tanvir from sales, waiting on the document, asked why it was late, and Vaibhav said, 'One line in the summary wasn't real.' I asked Vaibhav to note the check in the file so the next person does the same.

qa.q: How many figures and citations did the AI summary carry?
qa.a: It carried three figures and two citations.

qa.q: Why might Vaibhav feel uneasy trusting the smooth-reading AI summary, and what shows it?
qa.a: Vaibhav was wary that such tools sometimes invent things that sound right, so a smooth read was not proof.

qa.q: What could Vaibhav add to the checking, and why?
qa.a: Vaibhav could ask a colleague to spot-check two items, since a second pair of eyes may catch what a tired person misses.

qa.q: How might Tanvir have seen the delay?
qa.a: Tanvir was probably impatient waiting, but the reason shows the check kept a false line away from the client. 🙂

grounding: Shows an analyst checking each figure and citation from an AI summary against the original report before it goes into a client document.

subtopic: Using AI tools inside a team
passage:
Monday: After reading a news story about leaked company data, Vijay, head of a small design agency, emailed the team: 'No AI tools of any kind, effective today.' People nodded, a bit stunned.

Two weeks later: Deadlines were tight. Saurabh, a copywriter, quietly opened a personal account on a phone and pasted in a client's draft brief to get a rewrite. Others did the same and kept quiet; nobody wanted to be the one to tell Vijay.

Six weeks later: A client spotted a line in a document that matched text shared only in a private brief. Vijay learned that half the team had been using personal accounts with client files. At a meeting Vijay asked, 'Why didn't anyone tell me?' A designer answered, 'You said no. We still had deadlines.'

qa.q: What did Vijay's email say?
qa.a: It said, 'No AI tools of any kind, effective today.'

qa.q: What was Vijay afraid of when sending the email?
qa.a: Vijay was afraid of leaking company data, after reading a news story about a leak.

qa.q: What other approach could Vijay have used instead of a full ban?
qa.a: Vijay could have written a clear policy on approved tools and what data never goes in, so people had a safe way to work and no reason to hide it.

qa.q: How did the ban look to Saurabh and the others?
qa.a: It felt unworkable with deadlines pressing, so they used personal accounts quietly and stayed silent, since nobody wanted to tell Vijay.

grounding: Shows a manager forbidding all AI use out of fear, while staff quietly use personal accounts, creating hidden risk that a clear policy could have prevented.

subtopic: Using AI tools inside a team
subtype: Approach: sharing prompts and lessons in a team log [Action]
passage: Sit down, Yusuf. You asked how our team got good with these AI tools. Honestly, it wasn't the clever ones among us. When we started, three people knew the tricks and everyone else kept guessing. So I began a shared page. Whenever someone found a request that worked, they pasted it in with one line on why; whenever one failed, they pasted that too, and what went wrong. Every Friday afternoon, before chai, we read the page together for twenty minutes. Nobody was laughed at for a failure. Within two months, people who hadn't dared before were adding entries, and the same mistake stopped repeating. I'm Harish, and if you take one thing from me: skill kept in one head leaves when that person does.

qa.q: When did the team read the shared page together?
qa.a: They read it every Friday afternoon, before chai, for twenty minutes.

qa.q: What did Harish want when starting the shared page?
qa.a: Harish wanted skill to spread across the team instead of staying with three people, worried that it would leave with them.

qa.q: Which choice inside the story helped quiet members start adding entries, and why?
qa.a: Not laughing at failures helped, since it made it safe for people who had not dared before to share what went wrong.

qa.q: How might a quiet team member have felt before the page existed?
qa.a: They were probably unsure and a little left out, guessing while three colleagues seemed to know the tricks.

grounding: Shows team members noting prompts that worked and failed and reviewing them on Fridays so skill grows across the team.

subtopic: Using AI tools inside a team
subtype: Approach: protecting skills and learning of juniors [Thinking]
passage: With a client demo two days away and the office loud from renovation drilling, Avni still stopped at Minakshi's desk. Minakshi, a junior developer, had been pasting tasks into an AI tool and getting answers before reading the ticket. Avni worried Minakshi would reach the second year without knowing how the code worked. Over the drilling she said, 'New rule for juniors. Try it yourself first, even if it's rough. Then ask the tool to review it. And afterwards explain the code to me in your own words.' Minakshi frowned. 'That's slower.' 'A bit,' said Avni, 'but you'll be the one fixing it at midnight, not the tool.' They agreed to test it on one ticket that afternoon. The first attempt was clumsy, the review found two problems, and the explanation took ten minutes and showed one gap.

qa.q: What was making the office loud?
qa.a: Renovation drilling was making the office loud.

qa.q: What is Avni worried about?
qa.a: Avni is worried that Minakshi would reach the second year without knowing how the code works.

qa.q: What other approach could Avni add to protect the juniors' learning?
qa.a: Avni could set up a weekly walkthrough where each junior explains one piece of their code to a senior, since explaining out loud shows gaps quickly.

qa.q: How might Minakshi see the new rule?
qa.a: Minakshi found it slower and frowned, though the review and the explanation exposed a gap that may show its worth.

grounding: Shows a lead worried that juniors will stop learning fundamentals, so asking them to try first, use AI for review and explain their code.

subtopic: Using AI tools inside a team
subtype: Approach: incident review after an AI-related error [Revision]
passage: On Tuesday morning in the Mumbai office, the weekly sales report went up to management with a wrong number: the AI tool had put the eastern region's total at 4.2 lakh instead of 2.4. A manager caught it before it reached the client, but only by chance. Chinmay called the team together instead of hunting for someone to blame. They traced the path: the tool wrote the summary, Omkar pasted it into the template, and the reviewer checked spelling and layout but not the figures. 'We treated it like a finished document, when it's more like a draft from a colleague who sometimes gets things wrong,' Chinmay said. The team added a step where one person ticks each figure against the source sheet and updated the policy page with the new rule. Omkar volunteered to write the checklist.

qa.q: What did the AI tool get wrong?
qa.a: It put the eastern region's total at 4.2 lakh instead of 2.4.

qa.q: What does Chinmay's comparison suggest about how Chinmay sees the tool?
qa.a: Chinmay sees it as a useful but fallible drafter that needs review, and Chinmay seems calm and constructive rather than angry.

qa.q: What could catch errors like this even earlier?
qa.a: The team could ask the tool to name the source row for every figure, so the checker can compare each one quickly.

qa.q: How might Omkar have felt when the trace showed who pasted the summary?
qa.a: Omkar may have felt uneasy or responsible, though volunteering to write the checklist suggests a wish to help put it right.

grounding: Shows a team tracing how a wrong AI-generated number passed review, adding a verification step and updating the policy.

subtopic: Using AI tools inside a team
subtype: Approach: being open with clients about AI use [Action]
passage: Before the contract began, Sarita and Keerthana sat with the school trust's secretary in the Palampur office. Sarita said plainly, 'For the first draft of the newsletter we sometimes use an AI tool, and one of us always checks and edits every line.' Keerthana added that names, fee lists and children's details would never be typed into any such tool. The secretary was quiet, then asked what the tool would be used for, and Sarita showed a sample draft with the edits marked. 'Thank you for telling us,' the secretary said. 'Last year a vendor told us nothing and we found out from a parent.' The secretary asked for the promise to be written into the contract, and Keerthana added a line that same evening.

qa.q: What would never be typed into any such tool?
qa.a: Names, fee lists and children's details would never be typed into any such tool.

qa.q: What did Sarita want the secretary to see by showing the sample draft?
qa.a: Sarita wanted to reassure the secretary that a person checks and edits every line, so the secretary could feel confident the AI use was under control.

qa.q: What could the team do to keep the trust after signing?
qa.a: They could send a short note each quarter saying how AI was used, since repeated honesty keeps the promise alive.

qa.q: What would change for the secretary if the team had said nothing and the truth came out later?
qa.a: The secretary would likely feel misled, as with the vendor last year, and trust would drop, so no promise would have been written into the contract.

grounding: Shows a team telling a client where AI assists in delivery and confirming what data is never shared with tools.

passage:
Monday, 8 pm: A user posted a harsh review of Zeenat's budgeting app: 'useless, and the team doesn't care.' Zeenat's face went hot, and her thumbs began typing a reply about how many hours the team had put in. She stopped before pressing send and saved it as a draft.

Tuesday: Zeenat told Samir, a friend, about the draft. Samir said, 'You can post it tomorrow if you still want to.' By afternoon the draft looked sharp and defensive. Zeenat deleted it.

Wednesday: Rereading the review calmly, Zeenat noticed one real point: the reminder feature failed on some phones. She wrote a short reply thanking the user and promising a fix, then told the team.

qa.q: What did Zeenat do with the first reply?
qa.a: Zeenat saved it as a draft, and on Tuesday afternoon deleted it.

qa.q: How did Zeenat feel on reading the review?
qa.a: Zeenat felt hurt and angry, shown by her hot face and the reply she began typing to defend the team.

qa.q: What other approach could Zeenat use with a harsh review?
qa.a: Zeenat could send the user a private message offering help, since it avoids an audience and lets the real problem be discussed calmly.

qa.q: How might the user have seen the calm reply?
qa.a: The user probably felt heard and perhaps surprised, since a real fix was promised instead of a defence. 🙂

grounding: Shows a founder waiting a day after a harsh post before replying, so the reply is calm rather than an angry one written in the moment.

subtype: Approach: separating fair feedback from abuse [Thinking]
passage: After her cooking video was shared widely, Maria sat on the sofa with her laptop and read every comment, with Nazia beside her holding tea. Maria made three piles in her head and said them aloud. 'One: valid. This person says the timings in my recipe were wrong, and they were, so I'll fix them. Two: misunderstanding. Someone thinks I used a certain oil because I was paid to, and I can say I wasn't. Three: abuse.' A handful of comments called her names and mocked her accent. 'These don't get an answer,' she said. 'Answering feeds them.' She reported the worst two to the platform and hid the rest. The first pile she answered with thanks, the second with two calm lines. It took an hour, and she felt lighter.

qa.q: How many piles did Maria sort the comments into?
qa.a: Maria sorted the comments into three piles.

qa.q: How did Maria feel after sorting and answering?
qa.a: Maria felt lighter, having put the hurtful comments aside and dealt with the useful ones.

qa.q: What other approach could Maria use next time?
qa.a: Maria could ask a trusted person to filter the comments first, so she can fix real problems without reading the abuse herself.

qa.q: How might Nazia see Maria's way of handling the comments?
qa.a: Nazia probably sees Maria staying in control and looking after herself, and may feel relieved that the hurtful comments did not swallow her.

grounding: Shows a person sorting comments into valid complaints, misunderstandings to clarify and abuse to ignore or report.

passage: Advisor's note. On Saturday night I watched Tenzin, founder of a small delivery app, answer critics on a public thread. A customer had complained about late orders. Tenzin replied point by point, called the customer's numbers 'made up', and hinted that the customer was paid by a rival. Two others joined in. By Sunday morning someone had posted screenshots of the exchange on a bigger page; the thread drew more views than the original complaint had in a month, and three users wrote that they were leaving. On Monday I sat with Tenzin and Jasleen from support. I asked what the customer had actually said, and Tenzin found it was partly right about the late orders. We agreed Tenzin would stop replying for now and Jasleen would collect the facts.

qa.q: What had the original customer complained about?
qa.a: The customer had complained about late orders.

qa.q: What was Tenzin probably feeling while writing the replies?
qa.a: Tenzin was probably defensive and hurt, since every point was fought and the customer was accused of being paid by a rival.

qa.q: What could Tenzin have done instead of arguing?
qa.a: Tenzin could have replied once, thanked the customer, and said what was being checked about the late orders, without arguing over motives.

qa.q: How might the three users who said they were leaving have seen the thread?
qa.a: They may have seen a company that argues rather than listens, and doubted they would get help when something went wrong.

grounding: Shows a founder arguing point by point with critics and attacking their motives, so screenshots spread and the argument draws more attention than the complaint.

passage: In the support room of a ticketing software company, Santosh read a public post from a user, Sabina: the export button had wiped her saved filters twice, and no one had answered. The team gathered round Santosh's screen. Nobody wanted to argue. Santosh wrote the reply and the others checked it: 'Thank you for telling us, Sabina, and sorry about the lost filters. It's a bug on our side. A fix goes out on Thursday, and we'll post here when it's live.' On Thursday the fix went out, and Santosh wrote a second public reply confirming it and offering help to restore her filters. Sabina answered, 'Faster than I expected, thanks.' Two other users who had grumbled in the thread added thumbs-up.

qa.q: When did the fix go out?
qa.a: The fix went out on Thursday.

qa.q: How did Sabina feel after the second reply?
qa.a: Sabina felt pleased and a little surprised, shown by 'Faster than I expected, thanks.'

qa.q: What could the team add to catch complaints like this sooner?
qa.a: The team could assign someone to watch public posts every day, so problems get an answer the same day.

qa.q: How might the two grumbling users have seen the exchange?
qa.a: They likely saw a team that listens and follows through, and adding thumbs-up suggests their view had softened.

grounding: Shows a team replying politely, thanking the user, saying what will be fixed and by when, then following up publicly after the fix.
